unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding to weld to AWS specification (Alloy steel plate)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld low-alloy steel plate with manual metal arc welding (MMAW) to an AWS code and a welding procedure specification (WPS). You will learn why alloy steels harden and crack, how carbon equivalent, preheat, interpass temperature and heat input control that risk, and how to choose, store and use alloy electrodes. You will also prepare and weld plate in position, test and repair welds, control materials and records, and lead a team on alloy work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **MMAW of low-alloy steel plate** to the AWS code the Centre uses and a **welding procedure specification (WPS)**. Alloy steels are stronger, tougher or more heat- or rust-resistant than mild steel, but they are less forgiving to weld: the wrong electrode, a missed preheat or a damp packet can leave a crack that appears hours later.

In Jamaica, alloy steel plate turns up in bauxite and alumina plants (wear liners, chutes, kilns), sugar factories (boilers, pressure parts, mill parts), ports and wharves (crane and lifting gear), power stations, quarries and heavy machinery repair. Much of this work is done to a code, with records kept for every joint.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welders who already weld carbon steel plate in all positions with low-hydrogen electrodes, and who now work to a code on alloy plate, keep the records and lead others.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at Level 3
rows: Identify low-alloy steels from the mill certificate, and say why their heat-affected zone can harden and crack.
Work out the carbon equivalent (CE); set and check preheat and interpass temperatures; control hydrogen.
Measure and work out heat input; keep within WPS limits, especially on quenched and tempered steel.
Read alloy electrode classes; match strength and chemistry; store, issue and re-dry them correctly.
Prepare bevels, backing and tacks to the WPS; prevent lamellar tearing and restraint cracking.
Weld single-V butts on backing in the vertical (3G) and overhead (4G) positions with stringer beads or a narrow weave.
Know the procedure tests; find defects after the waiting time; repair to procedure.
Control fume, hot plate and preheating risks; keep plate, electrodes and records traceable.
Brief, supervise and record the work so every joint can be traced.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on alloy steels, CE, preheat, heat input, electrodes, hydrogen cracking, lamellar tearing, technique, testing, qualification, materials control and safety.

A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as carbon equivalent, martensite, Charpy, buttering, temper bead) and calculations; and longer answers that explain a method, a calculation or a plan.

**Group practical tasks**: 3G single-V butt test plates with preheat and heat input records and bend tests; and a plan from mill certificates (CE and preheat), a draft WPS, a 4G butt and a macro section.

blocks.note: The calculations in this unit (CE, heat input, travel speed, preheat bands) are quick marks if you practise them. Write the formula, put the numbers in, and check the units.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Alloy steels and why they need care

blocks.p: Plain carbon steel is mostly iron, carbon and a little manganese. A **low-alloy steel** has small, deliberate amounts of other elements (usually a few percent in total) to give strength, toughness, heat resistance or rust resistance.

head: Element
Main effect in the steel
Effect on welding
rows: The biggest single cause of hardening in the heat-affected zone
Strength at high temperature, hardness, rust resistance

head: Kind of steel
Typical use
Main welding concern
rows: Hydrogen cracking in the HAZ; preheat
Left unpainted; forms a tight, protective rust layer
Electrodes that rust to match, as the WPS gives
Boilers, pressure parts and piping that run hot
Parts that must stay tough when cold
High-strength and wear-resistant plate: chutes, buckets, liners, booms
Too little heat cracks it; too much heat softens it

blocks.p: The **heat-affected zone (HAZ)** is the parent metal beside the weld that gets hot enough to change but does not melt. If an alloy steel cools quickly from red heat, its HAZ can turn into **martensite**: a very hard, brittle structure. The more carbon and alloy, and the faster the cooling, the more martensite forms. Fast cooling comes from a cold plate, thick plate (which draws the heat away), a small weld or low heat input.

blocks.note: Mild steel has so little carbon and alloy that it rarely hardens dangerously. Alloy steel can harden so much beside the weld that it cracks on its own, with no load on it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Every plate has a **mill certificate** (mill test certificate) giving its grade, its **heat number** (the batch of steel it was made from), its chemistry and its test results.
The heat number is stamped or painted on the plate. When plate is cut, **copy the heat number onto every piece** before the marked piece is used up.
Alloy plate and mild steel plate look the same in the rack. Keep them apart, clearly marked, and never use unmarked plate on a code job.
If a certificate shows the steel is different from the steel the WPS was qualified on (for example more carbon), **stop** and check whether the WPS still covers it.

sections.title: Hydrogen cracking, carbon equivalent and preheat

blocks.p: **Hydrogen cracking** (also called cold cracking or delayed cracking) is the main danger when arc welding alloy steel. It needs **three things at the same time**:

head: Condition
Where it comes from
How it is controlled
rows: Moisture in electrode coatings; damp air and dew; rust, oil, paint and water on the joint
Low-hydrogen electrodes stored and re-dried as the maker says; heated quivers; clean, dry joints
Fast cooling of a steel with a high CE
Preheat and enough heat input to slow the cooling
Good fit-up, no over-welding, a sequence that lets parts shrink

blocks.p: Remove any one and the crack does not form. Hydrogen moves through the steel for **hours** after welding, so a crack can appear long after the welder has gone home. That is why the inspection plan waits a set time (often a day or two, as the code, WPS or plan says) before the final crack check.
Hydrogen cracks usually form in the HAZ, under the weld or at the toe, and run along the weld. In high-strength weld metal they can also run across the weld.
**Carbon equivalent** puts the hardening effect of carbon and the alloying elements into one number. A common formula is:
**CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15** (all in %)
Carbon counts in full; the other elements are divided because they harden the steel less than carbon does. The higher the CE, the more easily the HAZ hardens, and the more preheat is needed.
**Worked example.** A plate has 0.15 % C, 1.20 % Mn, 0.25 % Cr, 0.15 % Mo, 0.10 % V, 0.30 % Ni and 0.15 % Cu.

blocks.note: As a rough guide, steels with a CE up to about 0.40 seldom need preheat at normal thicknesses, and above about 0.45 preheat is usually needed. The WPS and the code's tables decide: never set less preheat than the WPS gives.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **CE**: higher CE, more preheat.

**Thickness**: thick plate draws heat away fast, so the joint cools quickly. A 50 mm plate needs more preheat than a 12 mm plate of the same CE. Some tables use the **combined thickness** of the plates meeting at the joint.
**Hydrogen level** of the electrode: lower hydrogen (for example H4) allows less preheat than higher.
**Restraint**: a stiff joint that cannot shrink freely needs more care.

flow: Read the minimum preheat (and any maximum) and the width of the band to be heated from the WPS
Heat evenly over the full band on both sides of the joint, with gas burners, electric heating pads or induction; keep a burner moving so no spot is overheated (on Q&T plate, never above the maximum)
Let the heat soak through; on thick plate check the temperature on the face opposite the heat where you can reach it
Check with temperature-indicating crayons, a contact thermometer or another instrument the Centre approves, at the distance the WPS gives
Preheat before **tacking** as well as before welding: tacks crack just as easily
Keep the joint at or above the minimum all through the weld

blocks.p: **Worked example (preheat band).** A WPS says: heat a band each side at least 4 times the plate thickness, and never less than 75 mm. For 25 mm plate: 4 × 25 = 100 mm each side. For 16 mm plate: 4 × 16 = 64 mm, which is less than 75 mm, so heat **75 mm** each side.

ul: The **minimum interpass** temperature is usually the preheat: if the joint cools below it between passes, reheat before the next pass.

The **maximum interpass** temperature stops the joint getting too hot over many passes, which coarsens the structure, lowers toughness and, on Q&T steel, softens the plate. If it is too hot, wait until it cools into range. Never cool it with water or a wet rag.
Some WPSs call for a **post-heat** (holding the joint warm for a time after welding) to drive out hydrogen before it cools.

Cr-Mo and some other steels need **post-weld heat treatment (PWHT)**: the whole joint is heated to a set temperature, held, and cooled under control, to temper the hard zones and relieve stress. The WPS gives the temperature and time.

If work must stop before a joint is finished, follow the WPS: keep the preheat on, or post-heat and cover the joint to cool slowly. Never just switch off and leave a part-welded joint to cool in the breeze.

sections.title: Heat input and quenched and tempered steels

blocks.p: **Heat input** is the arc energy put into each millimetre of weld. On a procedure test it is worked out for each pass from the volts, the amps and the travel speed:
**Heat input (kJ/mm) = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1 000)**

ul: Volts and amps are read from a meter (or the machine's arc display) while the pass is welded.
Travel speed = length of the run ÷ time taken. A 240 mm run made in 2 minutes is 120 mm/min.
More current or voltage, or slower travel (a wider weave is slower travel), means more heat input.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** 22 V, 140 A, a 250 mm run in 2 minutes. Travel speed = 250 ÷ 2 = 125 mm/min. Heat input = 22 × 140 × 60 ÷ (125 × 1 000) = 184 800 ÷ 125 000 = **1.48 kJ/mm**.

**Worked example (slowest speed allowed).** A WPS limits heat input to 1.2 kJ/mm. At 23 V and 130 A: slowest speed = 23 × 130 × 60 ÷ (1.2 × 1 000) = 179 400 ÷ 1 200 = **about 150 mm/min**. Any slower and the limit is broken.

head: Heat input
Effect on alloy plate
rows: Fast cooling: hard, crack-prone HAZ; lack of fusion
The properties the procedure test proved
Coarse grain and lower toughness; on Q&T plate a soft, weak zone beside the weld; more distortion

blocks.p: **Quenched and tempered** plate is heated, cooled fast in water (quenched) and then reheated to a lower temperature (tempered). This heat treatment gives high strength or hardness. Welding can undo it: if the HAZ gets too hot for too long, it is tempered again and **softens**, losing strength and toughness.

ul: The WPS gives a **minimum** preheat (against cracking) and a **maximum** preheat, interpass temperature and **heat input** (against softening).
Use stringer beads or a narrow weave, small electrodes and a steady travel speed; check heat input from volts, amps and speed.
Never flame straighten or heat Q&T plate beyond the limit its maker gives: it can lose the strength its heat treatment gave it.
Avoid arc strikes: on hard plate a stray strike leaves a hard spot that can crack. Grind out any strike and check it, as the procedure says.

blocks.p: In the **temper bead** technique each later bead is placed so that its heat tempers (softens) the hard HAZ left by the beads before it. It is used on some repairs where PWHT cannot be done, and only to a qualified procedure.
Low-alloy MMAW electrodes are classified like carbon steel ones, with a **suffix** for the alloy. Take **E8018-C3 H4R**:

head: Part
Meaning
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: 80 000 psi (about 550 MPa)
With the 1: low-hydrogen coating with iron powder; AC or DC electrode positive
Diffusible hydrogen no more than 4 mL in each 100 g of weld metal
The coating has passed a test for resisting moisture pick-up

head: Suffix
Alloy in the weld metal
Typical use
rows: 1¼Cr-½Mo boiler and pressure parts that run hot (usually with PWHT)
Weathering steel: the weld rusts to the same colour and protection
Higher-strength grades made to military-type specifications
High-strength and Q&T steels, as the WPS names

blocks.note: Always read the **full** class on every packet. E8018-B2 and E8018-C3 are both "8018", but one is a chromium-molybdenum electrode for boilers and the other a nickel electrode for tough structural work. The WPS names the exact class: use only that.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Match the weld metal strength to the plate (and the chemistry where the WPS asks, for example B2 for 1¼Cr-½Mo, W for weathering steel).
Use lower hydrogen (H4 rather than H8) for higher strength, thicker or more restrained work.
**Alloy plate to mild steel**, where the WPS allows: usually a low-hydrogen electrode matching the **weaker** mild steel, with the **preheat set for the alloy side**, which is more crack-sensitive.

head: Stage
What to do
rows: Dry, locked store, off the floor, labelled; oldest first
Holding oven at the maker's temperature (often at least about 120 °C); separate, labelled compartments for each class
Heated quiver, taking out only a few at a time
Only as long as the WPS or code allows, which is shorter for stronger electrodes (under the AWS structural code, for example, about 4 hours for E70XX and 2 hours for E80XX, unless tested for longer)
Re-dry at the maker's temperature and time, only as many times as the maker allows (often once); otherwise scrap
Scrap: cracked or chipped flux does not shield properly

blocks.note: Never warm electrodes on the hot plate, on the machine or in the sun, and never use an electrode that has been wet. Keep an oven log: oven temperatures, batches issued and returned, re-drying done.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Prepare the bevel angle, root face and root opening the WPS gives (for a single-V on backing, often a 45° to 60° included angle with a root opening to suit).
**Grind flame-cut faces back to bright metal.** A flame-cut face on alloy plate can be hard and may hold small cracks and oxide. Some WPSs ask for preheat for flame cutting too.
Clean the bevels and about 25 mm each side of all rust, scale, paint, oil, moisture and dew.
A **backing strip** melts into the root, so it must be the steel the WPS names, usually the same type as the plate. A mild steel strip can spoil the weld metal's make-up.
Run-on and run-off tabs, where used, are of the same steel and prepared like the joint.
Tacks get the **same preheat** and electrode as the weld: a cold tack on alloy plate can crack and the crack is then buried in the root.
Tack at the ends (or on the tabs), check the root opening, and clean and feather the tacks.

blocks.p: A joint that cannot shrink freely, such as an insert plate in a stiff frame or a heavy tee in a rigid structure, builds up high stress as it cools. That stress adds to the hydrogen and hardness, so restrained joints crack more easily.

**Lamellar tearing** is cracking under a weld in thick plate that runs in **steps parallel to the plate surface**. It happens when a large weld on the face of a plate pulls on it through its thickness, where flat inclusions left from rolling make the steel weak in that direction. Tee and corner joints with big welds on thick plate are most at risk.

head: Prevention
How
rows: Avoid large welds pulling through the thickness; use the smallest weld that is strong enough; arrange joints so the load is not across the plate thickness
Use plate tested for through-thickness properties (often called Z-grade) where the drawing calls for it
Lay a layer of tougher weld metal on the plate face before the joint is fitted up, so the joint is welded onto a sound, tough layer
Low-hydrogen electrodes, correct preheat, and a sequence that lets parts shrink and balances the heat

blocks.note: Lamellar tears are often below the surface. Ultrasonic testing (UT) finds them; a visual check may not.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Hold a **short arc**: no longer than the core wire diameter. A long arc lets air in and gives porosity, especially at the start.
Strike just ahead of where the weld starts, on the joint line, then move back to start the pool; or start on a run-on tab. This stops starting porosity.
Use **stringer beads or a narrow weave** no wider than the WPS allows: a wide weave is slow travel and high heat input.
**Chip and brush every pass** and fill every **crater** before breaking the arc: crater cracks (often star-shaped) start at open craters.
Check the interpass temperature before each pass, and record the pass data.

head: Position
Typical technique on alloy plate
rows: Root with a small electrode (often 3.2 mm or 2.5 mm), then fill and cap with stringers or a narrow weave
Stringer beads stacked from the bottom upwards; small pool; angle slightly up
Weld **uphill** with low-hydrogen electrodes: root, then fill passes with a slight weave within the WPS width, pausing at the edges
Small electrodes (3.2 mm for the root), very short arc, small even beads; stand to the side with full head and shoulder cover

blocks.p: On a procedure test, and on many code jobs, a recorder notes for each pass: the electrode class, size and batch, the preheat or interpass temperature, the current and voltage, and the run length and time, so the heat input can be worked out. On a procedure test these figures become the **procedure qualification record (PQR)** values that set the WPS limits.

ul: A welder's qualification record (WPQ) states the process, the steel group, the thickness range and the positions covered.
Generally, a test on thick plate (about 25 mm) covers a wider thickness range than a test on 10 mm plate, because it proves the welder can control many passes and the heat.

Positions on plate groove tests (generally, under the AWS structural code): 1G covers flat; 2G covers flat and horizontal; 3G covers flat, horizontal and vertical; 4G covers flat and overhead; **3G and 4G together cover all positions**.
A qualification can lapse if the welder has not used the process for the time the code gives (commonly six months).

blocks.p: A WPS for alloy plate is proved by welding a test plate while the values are recorded, then testing it. If it passes, the results go on the **PQR** and the WPS is issued with limits taken from it.

head: Test
How
What it shows
rows: A strip across the weld is pulled until it breaks
Whether the joint is strong enough
Ductility and fusion; side bends are used on thicker plate
A cut section is smoothed and etched
Fusion, penetration and the shape of the passes and HAZ
A diamond (Vickers) or ball is pressed into a polished section across the weld and HAZ
Whether the HAZ has become too hard: high hardness warns of cracking
Notched bars from the weld metal and HAZ are broken by a swinging hammer at a set (often low) temperature
Toughness: that the joint stays tough, not brittle, at the coldest service temperature

blocks.note: Steel gets more brittle as it gets colder, so Charpy tests are done at the temperature the specification gives, not simply at room temperature. Hardness limits are set in the specification (around 350 HV is a common limit in structural work).
blocks.label: Remember

head: Defect
Likely causes
Prevention
rows: Hydrogen crack in the HAZ, found hours later
Damp electrodes, low or no preheat (including on tacks), dirty joint, restraint
Dry low-hydrogen electrodes; full preheat; clean joint; good sequence
Arc broken without filling the crater
Big welds pulling through thick plate with inclusions
Current too low, wrong angle, weave not reaching the edges
Correct current and angle; pause at the edges
Long arc at the start of each low-hydrogen run
Strike ahead and move back; short arc; run-on tabs
Poor cleaning between passes; deep valleys between beads
Clean every pass; keep a good bead shape
Soft, weak HAZ on Q&T plate
Heat input or interpass above the WPS limit
Keep within the limits; stringer beads

flow: Mark and record the crack; stop the item moving on
Find the cause before repairing, or it will crack again
Remove the crack completely by grinding or gouging, shaping the groove so it can be welded
Prove the crack has gone with dye penetrant (PT) or magnetic particle (MT) testing
Preheat as the repair WPS gives: often at least the original figure, sometimes more, because a repair groove is highly restrained
Weld with dry electrodes from the oven, to the repair procedure, by a qualified welder
Inspect again after the waiting time, by the same methods, and record the repair

sections.title: Safety, materials control, records and leadership

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Fume from alloy electrodes (manganese, nickel, chromium and others)
Read the electrode's **safety data sheet (SDS)**; extraction close to the arc; respirators where extraction is not enough
Hot plate: preheated plate at 150 °C does not glow and looks cold
Mark it HOT, fence it off, handle it with tongs and heat-resistant gloves
Checked hoses and flashback arrestors; hoses kept off the hot plate; area clear of anything that burns; extinguisher
Set up only by a trained person; leads protected
Screens, the right filter shade, dry gloves and clothing, no wet floors
Lifted with the right gear, never by hand
Heat stress: preheat plus Jamaican heat
Water, shade and rest breaks; rotate welders on long preheated jobs

ul: Alloy plate marked and stored apart from mild steel; heat numbers copied onto every cut piece; certificates filed with the job.
Electrodes issued from the oven against the WPS, with class, size and batch logged; separate oven compartments; returns logged.
Any doubt about a plate or electrode: quarantine it until it is identified.

head: Record
What it holds
rows: Every joint numbered, with its welder, WPS, electrode batch and dates
Temperatures checked, when and by whom
Pass data (on tests and where required)
Current, voltage, run length and time, heat input
Results after the waiting time; repairs and re-tests

blocks.h: Leading a team on alloy work

ul: Confirm the WPS covers the plate grade, thickness, positions and electrodes, and that each welder's qualification covers the work and is current.
Check the plate heat numbers against the certificates, and the electrodes against the WPS.
Brief the team on preheat, interpass and heat input limits, the sequence, the waiting time and the safety rules.
Check preheat before tacking and welding, interpass between passes, and settings and cleaning as the work goes.
Arrange the inspection after the waiting time; record, repair to procedure and re-test before release.
Stop the work when something does not match the WPS: a different plate, a missed preheat, electrodes left out.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can say what makes a steel low-alloy and name the main kinds of alloy plate and their uses.
I can explain why an alloy steel's HAZ hardens, and what martensite is.
I can read a mill certificate and keep plate traceable by its heat number.
I can name the three conditions for hydrogen cracking and how each is controlled.
I can work out a carbon equivalent and explain how CE, thickness, hydrogen and restraint set the preheat.
I can apply and check preheat and interpass temperatures, and work out a preheat band.
I can work out heat input and the slowest travel speed allowed, and explain why heat input matters.
I can explain how Q&T steel is welded and why it has upper limits.
I can read an alloy electrode class, including the alloy suffix and the H and R marks.
I can store, issue and re-dry low-hydrogen alloy electrodes correctly.
I can prepare and tack alloy plate, and explain how to prevent lamellar tearing.
I can weld 3G and 4G single-V butts on backing with low-hydrogen technique and record the pass data.
I can explain the procedure qualification tests and what each shows.
I can name alloy plate defects, their causes and prevention, and repair a crack to procedure.
I can control the fume, hot-plate and preheating hazards.
I can lead a team on alloy work and keep the records.

terms: Buttering
Laying weld metal on a joint face before the joint is fitted up
Carbon equivalent (CE)
One number for the hardening effect of carbon and the alloying elements
Charpy test
An impact test in which a notched bar is broken by a swinging hammer
Diffusible hydrogen
Hydrogen that can move through the weld metal; shown by H4, H8 or H16 in mL per 100 g
Hardness survey
Hardness tests across the weld and HAZ on a polished section
Heat-affected zone (HAZ)
Parent metal changed by the heat of welding but not melted
Heat input
Arc energy per millimetre of weld, in kJ/mm
Heat number
The number of the batch of steel a plate was made from
Hydrogen cracking
Cracking caused by hydrogen, a hard structure and stress acting together; can appear hours after welding
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next pass is laid
Lamellar tearing
Step-like cracking parallel to the surface of thick plate under a large weld
Low-alloy steel
Steel with small amounts of elements such as nickel, chromium or molybdenum added
Martensite
A very hard, brittle structure formed when some steels cool fast
Mill certificate
The steel maker's record of a plate's grade, heat number, chemistry and tests
Post-weld heat treatment (PWHT)
Heating a welded joint to a set temperature, holding and cooling it under control
PQR
Procedure qualification record: the record of the test weld and results that support a WPS
Preheat
Heating the joint before welding to slow the cooling
Quenched and tempered (Q&T)
Steel hardened by fast cooling in water, then reheated to toughen it
Restraint
How far a joint is held so that it cannot shrink freely
Temper bead
Placing beads so their heat softens the HAZ of earlier beads
Weathering steel
Low-alloy steel that forms a tight, protective rust layer
Z-grade plate
Plate tested for its properties through its thickness

c1.title: Wear liners at an alumina plant in Williamsfield
c1.text: At an alumina plant workshop in Williamsfield, Manchester, Kemar is welding quenched and tempered wear-resistant liner plates into an ore chute. The WPS limits heat input to 1.5 kJ/mm. On one fill pass the recorder notes 24 V and 140 A, and the 300 mm run took 2½ minutes. Earlier, Kemar struck his arc on the face of a liner beside the joint by mistake.

c2.title: A boiler header at a sugar factory in Monymusk
c2.text: Sugar-factory maintenance in Monymusk, Clarendon, needs a section of a boiler header replaced. The plate is a 1¼ % chromium, ½ % molybdenum steel, and the WPS calls for a minimum preheat, low-hydrogen alloy electrodes and post-weld heat treatment. Joel, the Level 3 welder, has two joints to weld, and the shift will end before the second joint is finished.

c3.title: Mill certificates at the Centre in Spanish Town
c3.text: At a training centre in Spanish Town, a Level 3 group must plan a weld in 30 mm low-alloy plate. The mill certificate gives 0.16 % C, 1.32 % Mn, 0.15 % Cr, 0.10 % Mo, 0.05 % V, 0.30 % Ni and 0.15 % Cu. The WPS preheat table reads: CE up to 0.40: none up to 25 mm, 50 °C over 25 mm; CE 0.41–0.45: 50 °C up to 25 mm, 100 °C over 25 mm; CE 0.46–0.50: 100 °C up to 25 mm, 150 °C over 25 mm. During the weld there is a long break for a fire drill.

c4.title: A lifting frame at Old Harbour Bay
c4.text: Keisha is welding a low-alloy steel lifting frame for a fishing co-operative at Old Harbour Bay, St Catherine, with E8018-C3 H4R electrodes, as the WPS gives. The site has no rod oven, only a heated quiver, and it drizzles on and off all day. Some electrodes were left in an open packet overnight; the maker allows one re-dry. Small pores keep appearing at the start of each run.

c5.title: A procedure test near Montego Bay
c5.text: A fabrication shop near Montego Bay, St James, is qualifying a WPS for low-alloy plate for a cold-storage plant whose steelwork must stay tough at −20 °C. The test plate passed its visual check. In the hardness survey the HAZ reads up to 410 HV, against a limit of 350 HV. One face bend strip opened up along the edge of the weld, where the weld meets the bevel.

questions.q: What is the heat input of the recorded pass, and is it within the WPS limit?
o: About 1.12 kJ/mm, so it is within the limit
About 1.68 kJ/mm, so it is over the limit
About 1.34 kJ/mm, so it is within the limit
About 16.8 kJ/mm, so it is far over the limit
questions.why: Travel speed = 300 ÷ 2.5 = 120 mm/min. Heat input = 24 × 140 × 60 ÷ (120 × 1 000) = 201 600 ÷ 120 000 = 1.68 kJ/mm, which is above the 1.5 kJ/mm limit.

questions.q: Which change would bring Kemar's passes back within the limit?
o: Travel faster, with stringer beads
Weave wider so each pass covers more of the joint
Turn the current up and travel at the same speed
Use a bigger electrode so fewer passes are needed
questions.why: At these settings the slowest speed allowed is 201 600 ÷ 1 500 ≈ 135 mm/min. Faster travel, stringer beads or a lower current within the range all cut heat input; a wider weave or bigger electrode raises it.

questions.q: What should be done about the arc strike on the face of the liner?
o: Nothing, as it is outside the weld and will wear away
Paint over it so that it does not rust in the chute
Weld a bead over it to cover the mark completely
Grind it out and check the spot
questions.why: On hard Q&T plate a stray arc strike melts a small spot that cools very fast and becomes hard and crack-prone. It is ground out smooth and checked (for example by MT or a hardness check), as the procedure says.

questions.q: Which electrode class suffix suits Joel's 1¼Cr-½Mo header plate?
o: B2, as in E8018-B2
C3, as in E8018-C3
A1, as in E7018-A1
W2, as in E8018-W2
questions.why: The B2 group carries about 1.25 % chromium and 0.5 % molybdenum, matching the plate so the weld has the same strength at high temperature. C3 is a nickel group, A1 molybdenum only, W2 for weathering steel.

questions.q: Why does the WPS call for post-weld heat treatment on the header joints?
o: To burn off the slag left between the weld passes
To make the joint expand so it fits the old header
To dry the electrodes left over after the weld
To temper hard zones and relieve stress
questions.why: Cr-Mo steels harden strongly beside the weld. Heating the joint to a set temperature, holding it and cooling it under control tempers the hard zones, restores toughness and relieves residual stress.

questions.q: The shift ends with the second joint half welded. What should Joel do?
o: Switch off, cover the joint, and preheat it again in the morning
Let it cool quickly with a fan so it is safe to touch next day
Weld on with bigger electrodes at more current to finish today
Keep it hot, or post-heat and cool it slowly, as the WPS says
questions.why: A part-welded Cr-Mo joint left to cool without control can crack before it is finished. The WPS says whether to hold the preheat until welding resumes, or post-heat and cool slowly under insulation.

questions.q: What is the carbon equivalent of the plate on the certificate?
Using the WPS table, what preheat does the group's 30 mm plate need?
o: No preheat
questions.why: A CE of 0.47 falls in the 0.46–0.50 row, and 30 mm is over 25 mm, so the preheat is 150 °C. It applies to tacks as well as to the weld.

questions.q: After the fire drill, the joint reads 90 °C. What should happen before the next pass?
o: Reheat the joint to at least 150 °C, then carry on
Carry on, since the joint is still too hot to touch
Use a bigger electrode on the next pass to add heat
Weld the next pass more slowly to warm the joint up
questions.why: The minimum interpass temperature is normally the preheat. Below it, the next pass would cool fast and could harden and crack, so the joint is reheated evenly and checked before welding goes on.

questions.q: How should Keisha handle the electrodes she takes out to the frame?
o: Take a full packet out each morning to save trips
Keep them warm by laying them on the hot plate
Leave them in the sun so the coating stays dry
A few at a time in the heated quiver
questions.why: Low-hydrogen alloy electrodes pick up moisture once out of the oven; the stronger the electrode, the shorter the time allowed. Keep only a few in a heated quiver and return or re-dry them within the WPS or code limit.

questions.q: What should be done with the electrodes left in the open packet overnight?
o: Use them up first on less important welds
Re-dry them once, then keep them in an oven
Dry them in the sun for an hour before use
Re-dry them twice to be sure all the damp has gone
questions.why: Damp low-hydrogen electrodes add hydrogen to the weld. Because the maker allows one re-dry and these have not been re-dried before, they can be re-dried once at the maker's temperature and time, then kept in a holding oven. A second time out means scrapping them.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the pores at the start of each run, and the cure?
o: A long arc while striking; strike ahead, then come back
Too much preheat; let the plate cool before each run
Electrodes too dry; dip the tip in water before striking
Current too low; turn it up well above the WPS range
questions.why: Low-hydrogen electrodes give porosity if the arc is long while the coating's shield builds up. Striking a little ahead on the joint line, then moving back with a short arc, or starting on a run-on tab, cures it.

questions.q: What does the HAZ hardness of 410 HV tell the shop about its draft procedure?
o: The weld is extra strong, so the WPS can be issued as it is
It cooled too fast: more preheat or heat input is needed
The hardness test must be wrong, as alloy steel is soft
The HAZ is too soft, so the heat input should be cut
questions.why: Hardness above the limit means a hard, crack-prone HAZ from fast cooling. The procedure fails as it stands; more preheat or a higher heat input within limits slows the cooling, and the test is repeated.

questions.q: The face bend strip opened along the edge of the weld, where it meets the bevel. What does this usually show?
o: Porosity in the middle of the cap
The strip was bent round too large a former
Lack of side-wall fusion
Too much reinforcement left on the cap
questions.why: An opening along the fusion line shows the weld did not melt into the bevel face. Causes are low current, a wrong angle or a weave that does not reach the edges; pausing at the edges cures it.

questions.q: Why must the Charpy tests for this job be broken at −20 °C rather than at room temperature?
o: Cold bars are easier to break in the test machine
Room temperature tests always give a lower result
The notch can only be cut cleanly in cold steel
Steel gets more brittle as it gets colder
questions.why: Many steels lose toughness as the temperature falls. Testing notched bars at the coldest service temperature proves the weld metal and HAZ will not break in a brittle way in the cold store.

questions.q: Dwayne is preheating a thick joint with a gas burner. Why should he keep the flame moving over the whole band instead of holding it on the joint line?
o: So the burner nozzle does not clog up with soot
So the gas cylinder empties at an even rate
So the band heats evenly, with no spot overheated
So the joint stays cool enough to touch for tacking
questions.why: Held in one place, a burner overheats a spot while the rest of the band stays cold, so the preheat is uneven and, on Q&T plate, can pass the maximum. Moving it over the full band and letting the heat soak gives an even temperature to check.

questions.q: Which test is most likely to find lamellar tearing under a large tee weld before it reaches the surface?
o: A visual check of the weld cap
Ultrasonic testing
A dye penetrant test on the toes
A hardness test on the cap
questions.why: Lamellar tears run parallel to the plate surface inside thick plate, so surface methods often miss them. Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the plate and picks up the reflections from the tears.

questions.q: The holding oven has packets marked E8018-B2 and E8018-C3 in the same compartment. Why does this matter?
o: They are different alloys; the WPS names one
Both are 8018, so either may be used on any alloy job
Mixing them makes both pick up moisture much faster
B2 electrodes must be kept colder than C3 electrodes
questions.why: The suffix is the alloy: B2 is chromium-molybdenum, C3 is about 1 % nickel. Using the wrong one changes the weld's make-up and breaks the WPS. Each class gets its own labelled compartment and is issued against the WPS.

questions.q: Generally, under the AWS structural code, which plate groove tests together qualify a welder for all positions?
o: 1G and 2G
2G and 3G
3G and 4G
1G and 4G
questions.why: 3G covers flat, horizontal and vertical; 4G covers flat and overhead. Together they cover all positions. Always check the welder's own qualification record against the job.

questions.q: In a low-alloy steel joint, where is hydrogen cracking most often found?
o: In the slag left on the cap after the last pass is made
In the HAZ, often at the toe or under the bead
Only in the cap, where it is cooled by the outside air
In the unheated parent plate, well away from the weld
questions.why: The HAZ is where the steel can harden most, and hydrogen gathers there from the weld. Cracks often start at the toe or just under the bead; in high-strength weld metal they can also run across the weld.
